title: VA9-02277
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXX XXX XXXX (the "claimant") is a citizen of China who claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act").1 ALLEGATIONS
The claimant fears persecution because of his religious practices.
In 2004, he met his current wife, XXXX XXX XXXX, a devout Catholic. They started to attend services at an underground Roman Catholic Church. The claimant was baptized in XXXX 2005.
In XXXX 2006, the claimant married his wife. He continued to attend Bible classes.

In XXXX 2007, a police officer questioned the claimant about whether he was part of an anti-government organization, and warned him that he was under surveillance. The claimant and his friends decided to suspend their Bible study group for a while. It resumed meetings in XXXX 2008.
In XXXX 2008, a Bible study group being hosted in the claimant's house was broken up by the police, who arrested the worshippers.

The claimant was detained, questioned, threatened, and assaulted. He was pressured to write a confession. He was released on conditions including refraining from religious activities and reporting weekly to the police.

The claimant and his wife decided that they should leave China. The claimant was able to book himself into a tour of Singapore and Malaysia. His wife could not join him as she did not have a passport. He went to police stations in both Singapore and Malaysia and was advised that he could not make refugee claims.
Upon returning to China, via the Hong Kong airport, the claimant learned that his wife had been arrested. Therefore, he went into hiding until he was able to arrange exit with the help of an agent.
He entered Canada on XXXX, 2009 and made a refugee claim on April 20, 2009.
His wife remains in jail.

I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee in that he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in China. I also find that the claimant is not a person in need of protection in that his removal to China would not subject him personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and in that there are no substantial grounds to believe that his removal to China would subject him personally to a danger of torture. My reasons are as follows.
The personal identity of the claimant is established by the copy of his passport2 that is in evidence.

Regarding the credibility of the claimant, there is a presumption that sworn testimony is true unless there is sufficient reason to doubt its truthfulness. In this claim, the evidence raises a number of concerns about its reliability.

At the start of the hearing, the claimant amended his Personal Information Form, replacing the stated employment history. That history had been consistent with the information provided in his application for a Canadian Visitor Visa (CVV).3 The claimant allegedly obtained the CVV through the services of an agent and contained a false employment history.

The effect of changing the employment history is that the Personal Information Form (PIF)4 is now more consistent with the allegation that, due to fear, he used an agent to help him leave China. It is therefore a material difference. However, the change of information also demonstrates that the claimant is willing to sign his name to false statements. The PIF as originally provided, already shows handwritten corrections to the employment history, demonstrating that he had been aware of the information that he was providing to the Board, which he now states is untrue.

Secondly, the claimant states that he was in hiding after his return from Singapore and Malaysia, until he left for Canada, i.e. between XXXX 2008 and XXXX 2009. However, according to the information in his passport, he obtained a Singaporean visa in XXXX in XXXX 2009 and a Canadian visa in Beijing in XXXX 2009. This is not suggestive of hiding.

Thirdly, the claimant was asked questions regarding Christianity, such as whether he knew the "Lord's Prayer" and "Hail Mary" prayers. His recitations were rather garbled, which is quite understandable given the use of an interpreter. They were also very slowly and hesitantly delivered, which is harder to understand, given his alleged Bible study of several years. I also note that, while he could cite the religious significance of Christmas and Easter, he confused Communion with baptism.

Indeed, he testified that he has never been officially baptized and does not take Communion despite attending weekly church services in Canada. This testimony is inconsistent with the commitment implicit in his alleged attendance at and hosting of Bible study meetings even after the police told him to desist.

A fourth concern is that the violent treatment allegedly given to the claimant in detention, and the ongoing detention of his wife, is inconsistent with some of the country documentation regarding the treatment of similarly situated persons, that is, Catholics and/or worshippers at unregistered churches.

One report5 states that the relationship between the Chinese government and the Vatican has greatly improved over the last few years. Most, if not all, Chinese bishops appointed by the government-sanctioned Catholic association also seek Vatican approval. The state has officially given approval to the holding of religious beliefs, although there are still arrests and surveillance on underground churches. This source says nothing about the routine employment of violence against church members, however.

In another document,6 the US Department of State indicates that unregistered church members pursue their right to practice their faith through legal avenues, which have helped deter harassment from local authorities. I note that this view is disputed by a Canadian lawyer quoted in the same document, so this document is not being interpreted as giving an unequivocally optimistic opinion of religious freedom in China.

A more recent Board report7 states that there are about 14 million registered and unregistered Catholics in the country. One source indicates that Catholics can be arrested and fined, while another source states that there is a high degree of tolerance. Several sources have stated that they believe that authorities in Guangdong (where the claimant is from) and Fujian provinces might be more tolerant to Catholics than in other provinces.

In sum, the documents show that there is harassment of clergy and some worshippers, inconsistently applied, but also indications of tolerance, and little support overall for the allegations of being beaten and for the indefinite detention of the claimant's wife.

The fifth concern is that there is very little evidence that the claimant is actually married to his wife, the inspiration behind the religious activities that give rise to his alleged fear of persecution.

While there is no obligation that claimants provide corroborative documentation of their allegations, it is reasonable to expect that claimants who possess or could readily obtain such evidence would submit it for their hearings.

The claimant has allegedly known his wife since 2004, married her in 2006, and lived with her in the home of his retired parents. He has presented no photos, cards or notes from his wife. The claimant states that all of these materials were seized by the authorities for no reason. The circumstances of the marriage are odd, in that the claimant's parents and adult daughter were not present at the wedding.
The claimant's wife is listed in his application for a Canadian Visitor Visa (CVV), but, as already noted, he has admitted to making false employment statements in this document.

The claimant brought an untranslated document to the hearing, which he identified as his hukou, or household registration. The country document package indicates that the household register is a primary identification document in China which is issued by the police. There is legal obligation to list all of the occupants of the household.8

A translation of the document at the hearing revealed that the household occupants consisted of the claimant's father (head of household), mother, the claimant, his two brothers, a sister-in-law, and a nephew. The hukou was issued on XXXX, 1998, and updated on XXXX, 2010. The claimant's supposed wife is not listed in it.

The claimant's explanation for the absence of his wife from the document is that this is quite usual in China. When told that our country information indicates otherwise, he changed his explanation, stating that it is a problem for couples who initially come from different provinces to obtain accurate updates to their hukou. He averred that his wife lived with him from 2005, and that she is currently living with his parents and has been there since 2009.

Aside from there being no documentary foundation for either explanation, the claimant's answer raises a sixth credibility concern, which is that his testimony about his wife's whereabouts is utterly inconsistent with the allegation, stated in the PIF and never amended, that his wife "remains in jail."

This is a highly material inconsistency, since his flight from China was supposedly triggered by his wife's jailing and ongoing incarceration. On the evidence, I find that the presumption of truthfulness has been overcome. The claimant is not a reliable witness.
I have considered whether there is other evidence that could support his claim for protection.
There is documentation9 that the claimant attends church activities in Canada, but this does not address his experiences in China.

After the hearing, counsel for the claimant submitted a document purporting to be a mobile phone statement, billed to XXXX XXX XXXX at the claimant's address in XXXX City. This document is relevant. However, it has very little probative value, since it is a paper document issued by a private company, without any verification of its issuance, and provided by the claimant, who is not credible.

In sum, there is insufficient trustworthy and reliable evidence upon which I could analyze a claim for protection. Accordingly, there is no basis upon which I can make a positive finding under either section 96 or section 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

For the foregoing reasons, I conclude that XXX XXXX XXXX is not a Convention refugee and not a person in need of protection and I therefore reject his claim.
